introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 6 : dates de l'historiographie courante (victoire du Parti national de D. F. Malan en 1948, Suppression of Communism Act 1950, Sharpeville le 21 mars 1960, Rivonia 1963-64, Soweto le 16 juin 1976, résolution 418 de l'ONU sur l'embargo sur les armes en 1977, sanctions américaines de 1986, discours de De Klerk du 2 février 1990, libération de Mandela le 11 février 1990, élections des 26-29 avril 1994, Mandela président le 10 mai 1994). Le score exact de 1948 (majorité très étroite, avec le Parti afrikaner) n'est pas détaillé. Les deux parties de la question sont traitées : facteurs de l'institution, puis facteurs du démantèlement.

questions.enonce_markdown:
What factors influenced the institution of Apartheid in South Africa in 1948 and its dismantling in 1994?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Apartheid (Afrikaans for "apartness") was the system of racial separation and white domination set up by the National Party after it won the general election of 1948 and ended between 1990 and 1994 with the release of Nelson Mandela, the unbanning of the African National Congress (ANC) and the first multiracial elections. Its institution was influenced by the history of racial segregation, Afrikaner nationalism and the social and economic changes of the 1940s. Its dismantling was caused by long internal resistance, international pressure, economic strain, a change in the regional and world situation and the decisions of the leaders of the time.

**A. Factors which influenced the institution of apartheid in 1948.**
- *Earlier segregation.* Racial discrimination did not begin in 1948: the Natives Land Act of 1913, the Natives (Urban Areas) Act of 1923, pass laws, the colour bar in employment and the 1936 Native Trust and Land Act had already separated the races and reserved most land for whites. Apartheid extended and systematised this heritage.
- *Afrikaner nationalism.* Afrikaners remembered the Great Trek, the defeat in the South African War (1899-1902) and British domination. Organisations such as the Broederbond (founded in 1918), the Dutch Reformed Church (which supplied a religious justification for separation) and Afrikaans cultural movements built a strong sense of identity and a wish to protect the Afrikaner nation and its economic position, especially among poor whites. The National Party under D. F. Malan presented apartheid as a means of securing white survival.
- *Social and economic changes.* The industrial growth of the Second World War brought a large number of Africans to the towns, creating shortages of housing, strikes (such as the African miners' strike of 1946) and white fears of competition and loss of control. The Sauer Report favoured strict separation, while the Fagan Commission recognised that urbanisation was permanent; the National Party's "apartheid" proposal was a clear alternative to the government's uncertain policy.
- *Political situation.* The United Party of Smuts was weakened by the war, his links with Britain and uncertainty about native policy. In 1948 the National Party, in alliance with the Afrikaner Party, won a narrow majority in parliament under a system favouring rural constituencies, and it then used its power to pass apartheid laws: the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act (1949), the Population Registration Act and the Group Areas Act (1950), the Suppression of Communism Act (1950), and later the Bantu Education Act (1953) and the Bantu Authorities Act (1951) leading to the "homelands" policy.
- *International context.* The Cold War allowed the government to present opposition as communist subversion.

**B. Factors which influenced the dismantling of apartheid (1990-94).**
- *Internal resistance.* The ANC (founded in 1912), the Pan-Africanist Congress, trade unions and later the Black Consciousness Movement of Steve Biko and the United Democratic Front (1983) resisted the system through campaigns such as the Defiance Campaign (1952), the Freedom Charter (1955), mass protests such as Sharpeville (1960; the ANC and PAC were banned after it), the Soweto uprising of 1976 and the township revolts and strikes of the 1980s (including the Congress of South African Trade Unions, COSATU, from 1985). Armed struggle (Umkhonto we Sizwe, from 1961) and the imprisonment of leaders such as Mandela (from 1962-64) made the government unpopular at home and abroad, and the states of emergency of 1985-86 failed to restore order.
- *International pressure.* The United Nations condemned apartheid and imposed a mandatory arms embargo in 1977; there were sports and cultural boycotts, Commonwealth pressure, and disinvestment by banks and companies; the United States Congress passed the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act in 1986 over the president's veto. Sanctions cut off credit and technology and increased South Africa's isolation.
- *Economic pressure.* The economy was under strain from sanctions, military spending and the inefficiency of racial restrictions on labour; business leaders wanted a skilled and stable labour force and political stability.
- *Regional and world changes.* The independence of Mozambique and Angola (1975), the war in Angola and the independence of Namibia (1990) reduced South Africa's buffer of friendly states, and the end of the Cold War and the collapse of the Soviet bloc removed the argument that apartheid defended the West against communism.
- *Leadership.* President F. W. de Klerk decided in February 1990 to unban the ANC, the PAC and the Communist Party and to release Mandela (11 February 1990); negotiations (CODESA, 1991-92), an interim constitution (1993) and elections on 26-29 April 1994 followed, and Mandela became president in May 1994. Mandela's moderation and his willingness to compromise, together with that of de Klerk, made a peaceful settlement possible, and they shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize.

**Conclusion.** Apartheid was introduced in 1948 as a result of the legacy of segregation, rising Afrikaner nationalism, the social and economic effects of rapid urbanisation and the political success of the National Party in a Cold War setting. It was dismantled in 1990-94 because internal resistance, international sanctions and isolation, economic pressure, regional and world changes, and the courage and realism of leaders on both sides made the system impossible to sustain.
